If someone is submissive, it means they tend to give in to the will, authority, or wishes of others — willingly, without much resistance. A submissive person does not fight back, does not push their own agenda, and does not assert their own desires strongly. Instead, they go along with what others want, often putting other people's control or comfort above their own.

Think of it this way: imagine two people deciding where to eat dinner. One person says "Let's go to a pizza place." The submissive person, even if they feel like having pasta, simply says "Sure, whatever you want." Now extend that pattern to many situations in life — that's a submissive person.
What It Really Means — Going Deeper

Being submissive is about a power dynamic. It describes the person on the receiving end of authority or control, the one who yields rather than leads. The word carries the idea of bowing down — not physically necessarily, but in terms of will and decision-making.

A submissive person or animal or group tends to:

  • Comply with the demands or wishes of others, even without being forced
  • Avoid conflict or confrontation, often to keep the peace
  • Accept a lower position in a social, relational, or professional hierarchy
  • Defer (meaning: let someone else decide) rather than take charge

The key word here is willingly. Submissive behavior is generally not about being physically forced. It's about a disposition — an inner tendency or attitude — to yield to others.
The Spectrum: How Submissive Can Someone Be?

Submissiveness exists on a scale, from mild to extreme.

  • On the mild end, someone who is slightly submissive might just be modest, agreeable, or easy-going. They don't make a fuss. They go with the flow. This is often considered a polite or cooperative trait.
  • In the middle, a submissive person might consistently avoid standing up for themselves, let others make most decisions, and feel uncomfortable saying no. This can sometimes be a problem, because their own needs go unmet.
  • On the extreme end, a highly submissive person might allow themselves to be completely controlled by another — following orders blindly, never questioning authority, never expressing a personal opinion. This level of submissiveness can be unhealthy or even dangerous, especially if the person in authority is exploitative.

The word appears in many different situations. Here are the most important ones:

1. In Personal Relationships
A submissive partner in a romantic relationship is one who lets the other person lead — in decisions, rules, or direction of the relationship. This might be chosen freely and work well between two consenting adults, or it might be a sign of an unhealthy, controlling dynamic where one person dominates the other unfairly.

2. In the Workplace or Social Hierarchy
A submissive employee might never question their boss, always agree with management decisions, and never advocate for themselves — even when they are being treated poorly. While respecting authority is normal, being excessively submissive at work can mean you get overlooked, underpaid, or taken advantage of.

3. In Animal Behavior
This is one of the clearest and most widely used contexts. Animals, especially dogs, show submissive behavior when they are communicating that they accept a more dominant animal's authority. A dog rolling onto its back, lowering its head, or avoiding eye contact is showing submissive body language. This is a natural and important part of how animals establish social order in groups.

4. In Groups, Cultures, or Societies
Some cultures, institutions, or groups value submissive behavior — especially toward elders, leaders, or religious authority. In these contexts, being submissive is seen as a virtue: a sign of respect, humility, and obedience. In other cultural contexts, submissiveness — especially when it is forced upon a group (for example, expecting women to always be submissive) — is seen as unjust.

5. In a Spiritual or Religious Context
Many religious traditions use the word submissive to describe a believer's relationship to God or divine authority — a total surrender of one's own will to a higher power. Here, the word carries a deeply positive and devout meaning.
The Tone of the Word — Is It Positive or Negative?

"Submissive" is what we call a context-dependent word, meaning it can be positive, neutral, or negative depending on the situation.

  • Positive: A soldier who is submissive to military discipline, or a believer who is submissive to their faith, or a new employee who is submissive to learning from experienced mentors — these can all be seen as admirable.
  • Neutral: Two partners who have freely agreed on a dynamic where one leads and the other follows. No judgment is implied.
  • Negative: Someone who is submissive because they are afraid, have low self-worth, or are being manipulated or dominated by an abusive person. Here, the word suggests something problematic — that a person's voice, needs, and dignity are being suppressed.

In everyday speech, "submissive" often carries a slightly negative or cautionary tone — suggesting that the person lacks backbone, confidence, or the ability to stand up for themselves.
What Submissive Is NOT — Important Contrasts

Understanding what a word is not is just as important as understanding what it is.

  • Submissive ≠ Humble: A humble person recognizes their limitations and doesn't need to be the center of attention. But they can still firmly stand up for themselves or others when needed. A submissive person, by contrast, gives in even when they shouldn't.
  • Submissive ≠ Polite: Being polite means being considerate and respectful in manner. You can be polite and assertive at the same time. A submissive person may be polite, but politeness alone doesn't make someone submissive.
  • Submissive ≠ Cooperative: Cooperation means working together toward a shared goal. A cooperative person compromises and collaborates. A submissive person simply surrenders their will to someone else — there's an imbalance.
  • Submissive ≠ Patient: Patience is about tolerating discomfort or delay without complaint. A patient person is still capable of asserting themselves. A submissive person, however, may tolerate mistreatment not out of patience, but out of an inability or unwillingness to resist.

The direct opposites of submissive include words like assertive, dominant, defiant, and authoritative. An assertive person confidently expresses their own needs and opinions. A dominant person naturally takes charge and leads. These stand at the other end of the spectrum from submissive.

• "The new recruit was so submissive that he never once questioned an order, even when it seemed wrong."
  • "She had always been submissive in her marriage, letting her husband make every major decision."
  • "The younger wolf showed submissive behavior toward the pack leader by lowering its body to the ground."
  • "His therapist encouraged him to be less submissive and to start expressing his own needs without guilt."
Submissive describes someone (or something) that readily yields to the control, authority, or wishes of another — placing obedience, compliance, or keeping the peace above asserting their own will.
